author: Poetry Collection
title: Remembering That Day (Revised) by TJ Hamilton
content:
Pale days had long begun to stretch out


Until an effigy in motion forgot


About weeks and hours and better days


Without the tedious dinners for one.




The wife failed to see, as wives often do,


Frailties writ large across a husband’s heart,


Or maybe she’d believed since a little girl


In her man would beat a heart of steel.




Meanwhile,


To an unsouled effigy


It would all have been the same


To her, to me, and to all the others.




I might have persisted a while longer,


If I hadn’t had to decide,


How best to escape


The confusion of being a man.




Odysseus sacrificed to souls grown pale,


Bored with life in the world to come,


A drop of blood, an offering of life.


What else is an effigy to do?




* * *




Using “effigy” to represent depersonalization, and in this case depersonalization as a prelude to cutting my wrists, is courtesy of “Tranz” by Gorillaz.

author: Rob Wipond
title: A Biological Psychiatrist Wins the Nobel
content:
O

ne could be forgiven for feeling wary rather than celebratory this October when 

Stanford University neuroscientist and psychiatrist Karl Deisseroth

, along with two German scientists, 

received the Nobel Prize

 for inventing a new, invasive brain technology dubbed “optogenetics.”




After all, the last time a psychiatric treatment garnered a Nobel Prize for Physiology or Medicine was in 1949—for the lobotomy technique of severing the arteries into the brain’s frontal lobes. The award further boosted excitement among psychiatrists worldwide, who ultimately administered lobotomies to tens of thousands of people (often by, infamously, hammering an icepick through both eye sockets) as a “calming treatment” for hundreds of different mental and emotional conditions. Mainstream psychiatry later moved on from lobotomies with the emergence of new drugs. But 

protest campaigns

 led by family members of lobotomized patients continued for decades as they tried (in vain) to get the Nobel Foundation to rescind its award for a practice that had killed an estimated 5 percent of patients and left countless others permanently stripped of major emotional, mental, and functional capacities.




So, in 2026, is optogenetics biological psychiatry’s long-sought breakthrough for understanding and rectifying dysfunction in the mechanisms of the brain? Or is it another damaging, dangerous too

author: Matthew McWade
title: The False Promise of Patient Rights in Psychiatric Units
content:
I

 have been aware of patient rights since I began working as a Certified Peer Specialist in 2006. I had the privilege of serving as emcee at an M-POWERed event at the statehouse in 2009, and participated in testimony related to Massachusetts’ Restraint and Seclusion Initiative around the same time. I worked for a year at The Transformation Center, a wing of M-POWER, the now-defunct grassroots political organization that secured Massachusetts mental health patients their six fundamental rights on psych units. I knew each of the six fundamental rights by heart (humane environment, daily private visitors, professional communications, uncensored mail, phone access, and outdoor access), but after becoming a peer specialist, I rarely experienced psychiatric hospitalization myself and had little opportunity to see how well those rights were upheld.




During a manic episode in late 2025, I felt little fear about voluntarily admitting myself to my local psych hospital because I assumed my rights would be respected. After a single weekend, I was astonished by the poor implementation of the six fundamental rights, and my mental state deteriorated as a direct result of the psych unit’s inability to uphold even the most basic of those rights.

author: Ayurdhi Dhar, PhD
title: Being Mindful of Agony: How to Incorporate the Sublime in Our Daily Life—An Interview with Will Adams
content:
H

ow does a wounded world wound us in return? Can we be mindful and offer intimate attention to pain and trauma? We answer these and other questions with Will Adams who is an Associate Professor and Chair of the Department of Psychology at Duquesne University in Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania. He holds a PhD in Clinical Psychology from Duquesne and completed his clinical psychology internship at McLean Hospital, affiliated with Harvard Medical School.




Dr. Adams is the author of 

A Wild and Sacred Call: Nature-Psyche-Spirit

, published by SUNY Press, a book that explores the deep connections between human psychology, the natural world, and spirituality. His work brings together phenomenology, relational psychoanalysis, Gestalt therapy, transpersonal psychology, and contemplative traditions, particularly Zen Buddhism and Christian mysticism.




His scholarship invites us to reconsider the relationship between self and world, mind and nature, and psychological healing and spiritual life. In this very personal interview, we’ll be speaking with him about how a lifetime of contemplative practice came to his rescue during the most traumatic time in his life, the possibilities of a relational understanding of human and more-than-human experience, and what psychology might learn from contemplative traditions and our relationship with the natural world.

author: Ekaterina Netchitailova, PhD
title: I Refuse to Die; I Am Not Leaving
content:
P

sychosis is treated like a crime, and the sentence is social death.




There is no place in society for people like me. I’ve known it deep down for a long time, but I was ashamed to say it out loud. Having had a psychosis is treated as worse than having committed a crime. Few experiences carry as much stigma, and the shame doesn’t fade when the psychosis does.




For more than twenty years after my first psychosis, I was barking up the wrong tree. I believed the main problem was that psychosis was misunderstood. I thought that, at least sometimes, it should be seen as a spiritual or religious experience that goes beyond medicine, and not simply as a mental illness. I spent years trying to prove that nothing was wrong with me, and that I could do not only as well as those we call ‘normal’, but even better.




On the surface, between my ‘psychoses’, I look like a successful, capable person. I have lived in four countries, speak four languages fluently, have a PhD, am raising my son on my own, and have a job I love. In reality, every day is a battle, and the weight of performing ‘normal’ threatens to pull me under. What I really need is a break, something like a stay in a Soteria house, where people can go through a crisis in a calm, homelike place instead of a hospital. But instead of resting, I always chose to carry on. I felt I had to show everyone that I am capable, smar

author: Patrick William Kelly
title: The Person They Never Asked About
content:
A

fter lights out at the state forensic hospital, a worker would peer through my door’s square window every fifteen minutes. He would quickly flick the overhead light on and off—just long enough to record whether I was breathing and in what position I was sleeping. Sometimes I could hear him whispering the data aloud to a partner making rounds alongside him, recounting our bodily orientations like buried bodies in a graveyard:




Left side. Right side. Back.




They knew the position in which my body slept every fifteen minutes for ten months. But they rarely asked me a personal question about my life.




I spent fourteen months in county jails and a state psychiatric hospital after accepting a not-guilty-by-reason-of-mental-disease plea on eight felony stalking charges arising from a psychotic manic episode. I had a doctorate from the University of Chicago and a book with Cambridge University Press. I had also been misdiagnosed by four different hospital systems, prescribed the wrong class of medications for four years, and carried an undetected neurosyphilis infection that inflamed my brain while every clinician I encountered looked somewhere else. By the time I arrived at Mendota Mental Health Institute, Wisconsin’s forensic psychiatric hospital, in January of 2025, the system had demonstrated an extraordinary capacity to observe and document me and an almost total incap

author: Enrico Gnaulati, PhD
title: The Hidden Psychotherapy Drop-Out Crisis
content:
T

here is a psychotherapy drop-out crisis that the general public is largely unaware of and the mental health field apparently overlooks. 

Conservative estimates

 of the 

number of people who discontinue psychotherapy

 after starting hover around 28-33 percent, with well upwards of half doing so within the first few sessions. 

Trustworthy sources

 reveal that the 

median number of sessions

 received by people entering psychotherapy falls somewhere between seven and nine.




I call these estimates conservative because the way psychotherapy drop-out is typically defined and measured reflects medicalized models of short-term interventions aimed primarily at symptom reduction. 

Evidence-based treatment protocols

 considered adequate for improvement typically last 12-16 sessions, with 

a range of roughly 6 to 20 sessions

 depending on the type of disorder and its severity.




Admittedly, there are those people for whom a brief course of therapy aimed at symptom reduction is both preferred and satisfactory. However, it appears that such individuals are in the minority. 

A recent survey sponsored by the Psychotherapy Action Network (PsiAN)

 of more than 1500 adults in the U.S. found that 88 percent “Prefer therapy that may take longer because it helps you manage your symptoms and also addresses the root cause of problems.” Moreover, a substantial number of clients who

author: Richard Sears
title: Four New Studies Raise Concerns About Benzodiazepine-Related Harms
content:
T

his week, 

Mad in America

 examines four new studies around harms linked to benzodiazepine use. The first finds that benzodiazepines are linked to increased risk of heart failure and heart failure related hospitalization. The second reports that long-term benzodiazepine use (60 days or longer) is associated with worse cognitive function in people diagnosed with schizophrenia. The third finds that taking these drugs during pregnancy is linked to an increased risk of miscarriage. The fourth links benzodiazepines to increased risk of falls and fractures in older adults.







Benzodiazepines Linked to Increased Risk of Heart Failure




A new 

study

 published in 

Cardiovascular Toxicology

 finds that benzodiazepine use is linked to higher risk of heart failure and heart failure related hospitalization in people prescribed these drugs to treat insomnia. This research, led by Yi-Sin Huang from Taipei Medical University in Taiwan, also suggests that benzodiazepines are associated with a higher risk of heart failure hospitalization than other drugs used to treat insomnia.




The goal of this study was to examine the link between heart failure and benzodiapepine use in people with insomnia. The authors also wanted to compare heart failure outcomes between benzodiapepines and other drugs prescribed for insomnia. They conducted a systematic review and meta-analysis of previou

author: D.W.
title: What Psychiatry Missed: My Ferritin Level Was 6
content:
D

uring my late 40s, I began to experience bouts of utter exhaustion and brain fog, often around the time of my menstrual periods which were irregular. I would wake up feeling like I had not really slept and my memory was sluggish. There were times when even lifting a frying pan took a great deal of effort.




I spent much time on the couch during this time of the month, and did my motherly duties in spurts and with verbal instructions rather than being able to fully participate in the activities. I had experienced this at various times in the past, especially postpartum. Driving was a challenge, and familiar routes would no longer feel automatic as they had before. I would go to bed early thinking I just needed more rest, but at times I would not be able to sleep. My severe iron deficiency had not yet been identified.







I was already seeing a psychiatric provider, and I was waiting to see an endocrinologist because I had an autoimmune thyroid disease which had been diagnosed 16 years prior. I had moved and needed to wait for insurance to go through and get the referral. My mental health provider was a nurse practitioner and she thought I needed to take something for the insomnia and difficulty staying asleep.




Ambien was prescribed. I was told that it would help me fall asleep and possibly prevent waking up in the night. I started on 5 mg; the first month I took it o

author: Mat Costanzo
title: What We Seek in Therapy May be Lost to Time
content:
F

inishing my work day, I head home. I think about quickly changing clothes and going to the gym. I care about my health and value fitness. Yet, work was long and in the back of my head I know: I can always go tomorrow. As I turn the corner onto Skidaway Rd, I pass a large gas station. Unbidden, my mind rapidly recalls the food waiting in my kitchen. Nothing I’m particularly excited about. I don’t have ingredients, really. Only ready options like cereal, chicken cutlets, some packaged Risotto. I don’t really know what I’d do with groceries because beyond sauteed chicken and spinach or milk and cereal, I don’t actually know how to cook. I make a quick turn into the parking lot, jump out and am back in my car heading home with some hot chicken tenders. How convenient and delicious, I think.




It’s just myself and my dog at home these days. His needs are the only ones outside my own that place demands on me. So, after finishing my chicken, which I share with Petey, I put on some comfortable clothes and drive him to the dog park. I reflect on the strangeness of this obligation. There are so few left that haven’t been outsourced. I’m glad to be going, though. The dog park is one place I see people regularly. I look forward to seeing them. I used to work in person at hospitals and saw people there, but Covid changed that. I’ve worked remote ever since. Sometimes I consider it a bl

author: Yaakov Ophir, PhD
title: Let There Be Light: Before Psychiatry Writes Its Next DSM
content:
F

or all the years I have spent studying the DSM, the diagnostic manual so often called “the bible of psychiatry,” I never really stopped to think about that nickname. I assumed it referred to authority: the canonical text that tells clinicians what counts as a mental disorder and how it should be diagnosed.




But while writing 

my recent Feature for the 

British Journal of Psychiatry

1

 (a prominent journal within mainstream academic psychiatry), the metaphor suddenly struck me differently. Perhaps the DSM resembles a bible for another reason too. Its words have something of a “Let there be light” quality.




This is hardly a discovery of mine. Many of psychiatry’s most important critics were thinking along these lines long before I was. But working closely with the 

changing language of successive DSM editions

2

 made the idea strikingly concrete for me.




Psychiatric diagnoses, as 

Mad in America

 readers know all too well, are unusual things. They are largely classificatory constructs built around patterns of experience and behavior. We do not diagnose them through blood tests, brain scans, or other biomarkers that can independently confirm the diagnosis.




And that is what makes the wording so unusually powerful. Change a small thing in the definition, and watch what happens. Who meets the diagnosis changes. Which treatments are offered changes. What resea

author: Poetry Collection
title: The Arrogance of Man by Julia Caitlin Miller
content:
Trigger warning: Brief mention of rape and suicide.




Thighs soaked in period blood


I spent eight hours, free bleeding


Part of it in restraints, after a


Flashback to being raped


But, I don’t know how to articulate it


It’s just from the way a group of men


Grabbed, squeezed and held down my wrists


They were just following protocol


But, why don’t they think of this…


That restraints can be traumatic?




Once released, I stay in my room


Until I march to the nurses station


And wave my bloody underwear in the air


What do I have to do to get a pad around here?




Stamp on the label difficult


So much trauma, I can’t communicate it


In a language that humans understand


But, the doctor blames it all on bipolar disorder


I’m far gone, but not in the way he thinks


It’s all performance art


Song requests to the radio stations with dedications


Notes on the paper trash bags for the janitors


Notes on the paper menu trays for everyone in the kitchen




The nurse is the only one who gets me


My own Nurse Jackie


Because she’s on the same wavelength


And doesn’t misunderstand me


She doesn’t have the arrogance


Or stigmatize me the same way as my doctor


I told him I felt addicted to Effexor


He just said “that’s not in the literature”


As if books have all the answers

author: Chinedu Akpa
title: Marketing GLP-1 Drugs for Addiction: Why Critics Are Skeptical
content:
T

he enthusiasm surrounding glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists (GLP-1RAs) has moved beyond diabetes and obesity. Scientists are now investigating whether drugs such as semaglutide and tirzepatide could help treat addiction by reducing cravings and altering the brain circuits involved in reward.




There is a 

biological rationale

 for this idea. GLP-1 receptors are present in brain regions involved in reward, motivation, learning, and behavior. Early research suggests that GLP-1RAs may influence some of the same pathways implicated in addictive behavior.




But addiction is more than a biological process. It also has psychological and social dimensions. People may use substances or engage in compulsive behaviors to cope with trauma, loneliness, shame, anxiety, stress, or difficult environments. Recovery can therefore require more than suppressing a craving: it can involve developing new coping mechanisms, rebuilding relationships, changing one’s environment, and learning to live without the behavior that once served a psychological function.




That raises a question that has received less attention amid the excitement over GLP-1 drugs: if a medication reduces the biological urge to use a substance, does that necessarily mean it has treated the addiction? Or has it simply created an opportunity for the person to begin addressing the deeper psychological and social

author: Karin Jervert
title: Mad in the World at the Mad in Norway International Film Festival
content:
A

s a ‘voices and visions gal’, as I call myself, who recently reclaimed her life from psychiatric abuse and over-medication, every little life thing I do is so big and impactful that one of my friends at home has a running joke about me. She texts me after every event, trip, workshop, or talk and asks, “Are you changed?” and my answer is always “Yes!” because returning to life after losing so much to psychiatry has a mind-blowing impact even in the minutia others gloss over. Everyday things that “normal” people ignore, or feel are just living—to me are a miracle of sorts.




This is what I expressed at the restaurant when I toasted a room full of friends and colleagues in the Mad in the World Network who had come to Norway for a Mad in the World meeting and the Mad in Norway International Film Festival. Earlier in the day, a lot of jet-lagged folks sat around a room excitedly talking together about what would be possible in the future. At the restaurant, I spoke of the miracle of the moment we were living in just then, the fact that all of us arrived in person in Lillehammer to meet and to enjoy these films on rethinking mental health.




I looked around that room and saw my heroes. All fighting in their own way for the thriving, health, and sovereignty of people in mental distress around the world. To me, it was an epic gathering, the impact of which we will continue to se

author: Izzy Knowles
title: Don’t Let Barbie Out of the Glovebox – An OCD Account
content:
W

hen I was in fifth grade, I convinced myself I was pregnant. I had never even kissed a boy. A slight stomachache after guzzling down my morning glass of milk became the beginning of early-onset morning sickness. A fleeting urge for bacon at a time that wasn’t breakfast suddenly meant that I was experiencing a full-fledged pregnancy craving. I would look around the band room and stare at the other girls in my class, wishing so deeply I was them so I wouldn’t have to deal with this phantom baby.




The following summer, I was certain I had developed a powerful addiction to making my little sister’s Barbie doll, a foxy brunette called Nancy, do back walkovers. During a sixteen-hour road trip from Chicago to Vermont, I picked up Nancy and mindlessly began kicking her leg back over her head and onto my thigh. As I flipped her in circles over and over, I started to worry I would never be able to stop. I pictured a future bound to this motion alone, where the only escape would be a bedridden life with my hands permanently restrained to my sides. Terrified of the fate ahead of me, I cried and pleaded with my mother to hide the Barbie in the glovebox, out of sight.







By the end of sixth grade, I convinced myself that I was going blind (I couldn’t see in the dark), that my lung had collapsed (I realized I could breathe manually), that I was dying of cancer (I discovered a mole o

author: Brooke Siem
title: Psychiatric Drugs and Violence: What Can Genetics Tell Us? A Conversation With Selma Eikelenboom
content:
W

elcome to the Mad in America podcast. My name is Brooke Siem, and I am the author of the award-winning memoir on antidepressant withdrawal, 

May Cause Side Effects

. Today I am with Selma Eikelenboom. She is a forensic scientist at the Independent Forensic Services in Santa Fe, New Mexico.




Selma earned her degree from the College for Social Work in Amsterdam, Netherlands, in 1976, followed by 10 years of experience in psychotherapeutic treatment. She graduated from medical school at the Free University in Amsterdam in 1992 and worked eight years as a resident in surgery, emergency medicine, obstetrics, and internal medicine. From 2000 onward, she focused on medical forensics as the coroner for the city of Amsterdam and in the biology department at the Netherlands Forensic Institute, the state forensic laboratory.




In 2003, she started IFS with her husband, who is also a forensic DNA expert. In 2011, they moved to Colorado and opened a second laboratory. Through her forensic medical work, she became interested in the possible association between DNA variants, psychoactive medication, and violence. That became the emphasis of her work, leading to a research project with the University of Denver and a PhD in March of 2021.




In January 2021, she and her husband moved to Santa Fe, New Mexico. Currently, she is working as a forensic medical examiner investigating cases

author: Arianna Astuni
title: Lillehammer’s “Other” Olympics: The Mad in Norway International Film Festival
content:
T

hey arrive—amidst airline strikes, taxi strikes, train strikes, airport closures, heavy luggage woes, and all the other obstacles that make traveling a challenge—in Lillehammer, Norway.




Photo by Kermit Cole




It doesn’t elude me that the small Norwegian town that hosted the big Olympics welcomes this group. They arrive ready to win, too. Their whole lives are about fighting to win—winning back lives and winning back the truth. This is a celebration, not of a finished goal—their work will be forever—but of notches in belts and the realization that they are not alone in this battle. They come mad, from every country, their own Olympics, to change the practices of antiquated psychiatry and views on mental illness and over-medication of those deemed mentally ill.




As an American, Lillehammer is synonymous with Tonya Harding and Nancy Kerrigan. As a human, madness is synonymous with King Lear, the Mad Hatter, the Joker, and Charles Manson. The consequence of the caricature. The evil of an individual. Contention rules our definition of things we don’t know. And things that scare us are “othered.” We wait hopefully for them to be tempered and extinguished. They are systematically silenced through practice and language.




Foucault says language is not a neutral tool. It is the means through which power shapes how we think and act, and even what we can know. It’s a device

author: Peter C. Gøtzsche, MD
title: Didn’t Anyone Tell You It Is Okay to Be Different?
content:
T

he Mad in Norway film festival took place in Lillehammer, 24-26 September. It was a remarkable experience. The participants came from many parts of the world and counted psychiatrists, psychologists, other health professionals, filmmakers, musicians, other artists, and previous and current patients.




It struck me that, despite all the diversity, people agreed that mental health needs to be systematically reformed, with more emphasis on psychosocial interventions, as was 

recently recommended

 by the United Nations and the World Health Organization. What I felt the strongest during the festival was how rewarding it was to interact with so many kind people who could think for themselves and look through the drug industry propaganda.




Photo of the Mad in Norway Film Festival by Kermit Cole




The stories I heard during the breaks confirmed how harmful drug focused psychiatry is. A German woman told me she lost her husband three years earlier. After they tripled the dose of his antidepressant, he developed adverse effects. In response, they also tripled his dose of olanzapine, and he died two days later.




Another German woman told me she became diagnosed with anxiety and depression after she had been prescribed a birth control pill as a teenager. Depression is a well-known harm of such pills described in the package inserts. This led to treatment with an SSRI. When s

author: Robert Whitaker
title: The New York Times Fails Our Veterans
content:
O

n September 28, the 

NY Times

 published a 

short article 

titled “VA Institutes New Consent Requirements for Some Psychiatric Drugs.” While the article is of little lasting import, reviewing it does provide an opportunity to reveal how the newspaper constructed a story that is protective of the conventional narrative of helpful psychiatric drugs, and while doing so commits what can only be described as journalistic malpractice.




The Historical Context




The VA’s mandate, which will require VHA doctors to obtain written consent when prescribing antidepressants to veterans under 30 years of age, is simply the latest development—and a small development at that—in a much larger story that dates back to at least 2006, when the VA launched a focused suicide prevention effort.




Around that time, Veteran Health Administration facilities began regularly screening veterans for depression, PTSD and substance use. This screening naturally led to a steady increase in the percentage of veterans diagnosed with a psychiatric disorder and treated with psychiatric drugs.







This initiative was expected to decrease suicides in veterans. Instead, suicides among veterans accessing VHA facilities steadily rose. So too disability rates among veterans, which 

more than doubled 

from 2010 to 2024.







In response, there arose within the veteran community the feeling that this t

author: Poetry Collection
title: A War Song to the Person Who Told Me to Die by Raine Ajani
content:
I just thought you should know I’m doing okay now,


I’m shielded by hardened sweat and scum,


Wielding a sword of my broken fingernails,


Voice rupturing with my vengeful war song.




I am forged by the failure to be perfect,


The pressure to exist with precision cracks my knees,


Self-assured strides callous my feet,


All while being told to die.




I just thought you should know what I’ve been through,


Furious deserts and loveless tundra,


The sweet, prickly fruit of addiction,


The ice shards of words I’ll never forget.




Since the last time I saw you,


I’ve been pricked by needles,


Forced to breathe acid-laced air,


Draped in blue scrubs,


And drugged to the point of stability.




I found my dignity in the fetal position,


I needed my breasts to warm my chest,


Needed to put my head to my knees…


To cry,


To think,


To let the spite bubble like stomach acid.




I just thought you should know what I wish for the future,


Black ink shaped to form the letters of my name,


The hard edges of words,


Words I’ll write,


Words that hug and choke my readers,


And make you regret your cruelty.




I hope your regret castrates you and your confidence.




I just thought you should know how your wish for my death used to make me want to grant it,


I thought death could make me feel seen,


Make me a scene on the city block,


For what screams see me more

author: Bruce Levine, PhD
title: Getting Rid of the Pain Before Answering Its Questions: Psychiatry’s Damage to Self and Culture
content:
“If you get rid of pain before you have answered its questions, you get rid of the self along with it.”


—Lewis Hyde, 

Alcohol and Poetry: John Berryman and the Booze Talking

, 1975.




P

eople come to mental health professionals in pain—the pain of anxiety, depression, substance abuse, inattention, and a variety of other mental pains. Psychiatric “treatment” routinely is directed at getting rid of these pains as quickly as possible so that an individual can “function.”




In this sense, we should be grateful that psychiatric treatment has been such a failure, a reality that has now even been acknowledged by some in the mainstream media including the 

New York Times

, which 

concluded

 in 2021: “Almost every measure of our collective mental health—rates of suicide, anxiety, depression, addiction deaths, psychiatric prescription use—went the wrong direction, even as access to services expanded greatly.”




Had psychiatric treatment been more successful in getting rid of pain before its questions were answered, the struggle for authentic self and a healing culture could well have been lost; as it is, those of us who care about such are only losing the struggle, but we have not been completely defeated.




Psychiatry’s Damage to the Authentic Self and a Healing-System Culture

author: Forrest Wolfe
title: Meeting Persephone: A Katabasis of Bipolar Night
content:
I

n the Greek Eleusinian mysteries, Persephone was the maiden abducted by Hades. She became the ineffable queen of the underworld whose name must not be spoken. One archaic root of her name, 

phónos

, means “murder.” Her abduction was also her death. Yet in the ancient Mediterranean world, pilgrims traveled to Eleusis seeking an epiphany of her that might inspire hope for the soul’s return.




Two and a half decades ago, in the crisis of my first psychotic collapse, I met Persephone.




The seeds of that encounter were prefigured by the memory of a woman—for whom I had no right to feel anything beyond the measure of our brief encounter. Just a few meetings and conversations around my hometown of East Northport, Long Island, after college. Something she said struck me, about going to nursing school because “that is the only thing I am any good at.” An intuition of a saintly meaning in her words, which would otherwise have seemed banal. Then I went away to film school in Los Angeles. I was twenty-three.




Can we live our stories forward into the unknown and recover them in the afterlife of memory—like a dying person gathering his tales? After my psychic collapse, five years later, I would write of this underestimated encounter with the woman whose name I shall encipher here as N: “In all possible worlds, I met her. In all possible worlds, I lost her. Madness is but a door

author: Martin Plöderl, PhD
title: From Efficacy to Non-Efficacy: Lessons from Pediatric Fluoxetine Trials
content:
F

luoxetine is recommended as a first-line antidepressant to treat pediatric depression in major guidelines, and it is one of the most widely prescribed antidepressants for children and adolescents. However, modern studies find that fluoxetine has lost its efficacy and can now be considered clinically equivalent to placebo. In this piece, I will explain this puzzling phenomenon, which is also crucial for judging the efficacy of other common antidepressants. This issue has not yet been adequately addressed, which can lead to potential harm for young patients.

Fluoxetine’s loss of efficacy




Two influential reviews published in 2016 and 2020 in prestigious 

Lancet

 journals 

[1,2]

Fluoxetine is probably the best option to consider when a pharmacological treatment is indicated.”
